strengths: Addresses important gap in VLM explainability rather than just accuracy, filling a genuine need in reasoning chain evaluation
High-quality expert-curated dataset with 800 reasoning chains from world champion and professional GeoGuessr players, providing credible ground truth
Comprehensive and systematic error analysis with clear categorization of failure modes (hallucination, misattribution, false tool use, axiomatic irrelevance) supported by concrete examples
Three complementary evaluation methodologies (LLM-as-a-judge variants) with thoughtful design showing methodological exploration
Extensive reproducibility support with detailed prompts, algorithms, guidelines in appendices and open-source commitment
Thorough coverage evaluating 8+ VLMs across open-weight and proprietary categories, providing comparative insights
Insightful observation about small-pixel features being overlooked by VLMs despite high resolution, pointing to vision encoder limitations
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology concern: one-to-all LLM-as-a-judge achieves lower MAE than human grading (12.06 vs implied higher), raising questions about judge calibration and whether automated judge is properly validated
Limited human validation with only 150 reasoning chains across 75 locations for calibration; inter-annotator agreement not reported, making gold standard reliability unclear

Non-exhaustiveness of expert chains creates fundamental evaluation ambiguity—alternative-but-valid reasoning paths may be unfairly penalized by precision/recall framework that assumes one-to-one correspondences

Prompt sensitivity unexamined: identical prompts used across all VLMs with acknowledged but unexplored limitation; no ablation studies on how different prompt formulations affect results across model types

Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates; inconsistency in reporting hallucinated baseline (27.14 vs 18.48 in Table 2); extreme baseline ceiling/floor effects suggest poor discrimination

Computational limitations affecting completeness: insufficient compute for largest open-weight models (Gemma-3-27B, Qwen3-VL-235B), potentially underrepresenting best open-weight capabilities and weakening claims about open vs proprietary gaps
Domain-specific scope limits generalization: findings tightly coupled to geolocation/Google Street View; unclear how insights transfer to other reasoning chain evaluation tasks or domains
English-only reasoning chains with no validation of multilingual generalization or cultural variations in reasoning patterns
Missing downstream validation: claims about explanations teaching non-experts are unsupported by human study; no empirical evidence that reasoning chain quality affects human understanding or trust
Practical justification incomplete: unclear why reasoning quality matters when VLMs achieve high geolocation accuracy; no analysis of downstream impacts of poor reasoning chains

strengths: Dataset of 800 expert reasoning chains from world-class GeoGuessr players is a valuable resource
Systematic characterization of VLM failure modes with compelling examples (hallucination, misattribution, false tool use, fine-grained detail omission)
Comprehensive multi-model evaluation comparing both open-weight and proprietary VLMs
Good empirical scope with detailed metrics (precision, recall, F1) across 800 chains and multiple geographic regions
Well-written paper with clear organization and high-quality visualizations
Useful error taxonomy that provides actionable insights into VLM limitations
weaknesses: Critical validity issue: only 150/800 chains (18.75%) human-graded, with single annotators per chain and no inter-rater reliability reported—insufficient to establish ground truth
Non-exhaustive ground truth fundamentally undermines the benchmark: VLMs providing alternative but valid reasoning paths are penalized, making it impossible to distinguish 'wrong' from 'different'
Major unexamined confound: fixed prompt across all VLMs; authors acknowledge prompt tuning could substantially improve performance but provide no ablations, artificially depressing scores
Automated judgment validation is weak: only 75 locations (225 pairs) used to validate judging methods; MAE of 12 points on 100-point scale without justification of acceptability
Questionable relevance to ACL: geolocation is primarily a computer vision task; better fit would be CVPR/ICCV or multimodal venues with limited implications for NLP community
Small human evaluation set for validating automated judges raises concerns about reliability; no bootstrap confidence intervals or significance tests on model differences
Reproducibility concerns: results depend on temporal snapshots of models (e.g., Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507), API availability, and specific prompt formulations
Missing ablations on critical design choices: expert selection effects, ground truth set size, algorithm hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., 0.45 cosine threshold in Algorithm 2 appears ad-hoc)
Limited novelty: error categorization is unsurprising (hallucinations in VLMs are well-known); LLM-as-judge methodology is derivative; findings lack depth beyond empirical characterization
Circular evaluation concern: using Qwen models as both candidates and evaluators could introduce bias; no analysis of judge model robustness
Open-sourcing claims unverifiable: paper states code/data will be released but only provides placeholder links
Incomplete analysis: strong correlation between F1 and country accuracy (Figure 6) suggests benchmark may measure location prediction more than reasoning quality

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing the explainability gap in VLMs for geolocation—an important issue for trustworthy AI systems
High-quality expert dataset curated with elite GeoGuessr players (including world champion), featuring non-exhaustive and natural reasoning chains
Comprehensive evaluation methodology with three complementary judging approaches and calibration against human grading
Well-articulated error taxonomy (misattribution, hallucination, false tool use, etc.) with compelling qualitative examples that provide actionable insights
Broad empirical coverage across open-weight and proprietary VLMs, with striking finding that open-weight models perform near hallucinated baseline
Detailed algorithms and clear experimental setup supporting reproducibility; commitment to open-source the benchmark
Effective presentation with clear figures and well-structured argumentation
Systematic analysis of fine-grained visual details overlooked by VLMs (Figure 8) with implications for vision encoding improvements
weaknesses: Missing inter-annotator agreement metrics (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha) despite multiple annotators, undermining evaluation rigor. Expert country-level accuracy variance (90-97%) deserves explicit analysis
Small human grading sample (150 locations, 3 annotators) for calibrating automated judges; MAE of 12-13 between judging methods indicates non-trivial disagreement
One-to-all bipartite strategy presented without justification or comparison to alternatives; grading guidelines permit subjective 'lenient scoring' for coarse-to-fine reasoning
Limited dataset scope: 500 unique images constrained to GeoGuessr/Google Street View, English only, geographically biased by coverage; generalization to other contexts unclear

Insufficient technical justification for key choices: Why Qwen-3 as LLM judge? No comparative analysis with other LLM judges; threshold hyperparameter (0.45) lacks sensitivity analysis; prompt engineering (Figure 14) sensitivity unexplored
Expert reasoning disagreement not quantified: only 150 shared locations among 3 experts; expert-to-expert agreement on shared images not reported
Incomplete comparison with prior work (GeoReasoner, GeoChain): no direct empirical comparison or explicit contrast of why unconstrained chains are superior

Error categorization (Section 4.5) is qualitative without quantitative frequency breakdown; no analysis of which attribute categories (Figure 3) are most critical; weak exploration of why open-weight F1 (~24-31) barely exceeds hallucinated baseline (~27)

strengths: Well-motivated task addressing an important gap between VLM geolocation accuracy and reasoning explainability, with clear applications to forensics and OSINT
Rigorous benchmark construction with expert annotations from credentialed domain specialists and clear annotation protocols with detailed guidelines
Calibrated evaluation methodology with human expert grading separate from chain authorship, three systematic automated approaches, and inter-annotator agreement metrics (ICC 0.787-0.917)
Comprehensive experimental scope benchmarking 8+ VLMs revealing clear performance stratification between proprietary and open-weight models

Insightful qualitative error analysis with five well-characterized failure categories (geographic misattribution, hallucination, false tool use, axiomatic irrelevance, missed details) illustrated with concrete examples
Effective visual ablation (Figure 25) supporting the lossy image encoding hypothesis with high-resolution vs. downsampled comparisons
Useful resource contribution that will benefit the community; dataset and benchmark framework enable future research on VLM reasoning
weaknesses: Moderate correlation between automated and human evaluation (Pearson r=0.689 for best method) limits confidence in automated scoring, particularly for the 750 chains not human-graded
Limited scale and annotator diversity with only 3 expert annotators and 150 chains (18.75%) human-evaluated; no inter-expert agreement reported for reasoning chain quality itself
Error analysis lacks quantification—five error categories are identified qualitatively but without frequency distributions, making it difficult to prioritize which failures to address
Fundamental asymmetry in evaluation conditions: experts write non-exhaustive chains while VLMs are prompted for 'detailed explanation,' creating an unequal comparison
Absence of statistical significance testing for main results; the 12-point F1 gap between best VLM (43.74%) and human average (56.69%) reported with point estimates only
Limited generalizability analysis—findings may be specific to geolocation with fine-grained visual details; no exploration of whether insights transfer to other reasoning tasks or geographic regions
No proposed solutions to identified problems; paper is purely diagnostic without methodological or training contributions to improve VLMs
Incomplete investigation of key findings—e.g., open-weight VLMs score only marginally above the hallucinated baseline (18.13 F1), suggesting possible stereotype memorization, but this is not explored

Methodological choices incompletely justified: one-to-all selected over keypoints approach based on MAE and Pearson despite keypoints slightly outperforming on Spearman/Kendall (Table 4); tuning process for hyperparameters not described
Fixed prompts across all VLMs acknowledged as limitation; no exploration of prompt engineering effects or model-specific optimization, which could significantly affect results

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses important explainability gap in geolocation reasoning, motivated by real-world applications (forensics, OSINT)
High-quality expert dataset: Curated from champion-tier GeoGuessr players (top 0.01%) following rigorous annotation protocol with detailed guidelines
Rigorous evaluation methodology: Multiple evaluation approaches (one-to-all, key-points, VLM-based) validated against human grading with inter-annotator agreement metrics
Comprehensive benchmarking: Evaluates 9+ VLMs across open and proprietary models with detailed results, confidence intervals, and thorough error analysis
Systematic error taxonomy: Clear categorization of failure modes (misattribution, hallucination, false tool use, axiomatic irrelevance, missed details) with concrete examples
Reproducibility commitment: Promises to open source benchmark and code; detailed appendices with prompts, algorithms, and guidelines
weaknesses: Concerning human baseline: Expert F1 score of 56 is troublingly low; high ICC3k agreement (0.917) contradicts this, suggesting either methodological issues or task subjectivity that undermines 'ground truth' concept
Limited scale and scope: 500 images is modest for 2026 benchmark; small dataset limits representativeness and generalizability across geolocation contexts
Weak fit for ACL: Paper admits core challenge is vision-based (fine-grained visual attribute extraction); limited linguistic innovation or insights for NLP audience; better suited for CVPR/ICCV
Limited evaluation novelty: Evaluation methods are straightforward applications of existing LLM-as-a-judge approaches; no novel contribution to evaluation methodology; simplistic algorithm designs

Experimental design concerns: Fixed prompts across models (acknowledged limitation not addressed); inconsistent hyperparameters (max_new_tokens: 512-32,768) compromise fair comparison; no ablation studies on design choices

Missing critical analyses: No correlation study between reasoning quality and geolocation accuracy; no downstream task evaluation; error taxonomy is qualitative, not quantitative; lacks systematic attribute-level analysis of VLM failures
Unresolved methodological question: Low human F1 (56) poorly explained—if expert chains don't match each other well, what validates 'ground truth' status? This fundamental issue needs resolution
Limited constructiveness: Problem identification is clear but solutions vague ('improve vision encoding'); no proposed methods, mitigation strategies, or failure case guidance for future work
Missing comparisons: No empirical comparison with related datasets (GeoComp, GeoChain, GeoExplain, GeoReasoner) despite detailed related work section; unclear if benchmark will be adopted

Reproducibility concerns: Grading guidelines explicitly acknowledge subjectivity ('be lenient'); hyperparameters appear tuned on evaluation set; no inter-rater reliability for individual chains; wide confidence intervals raise precision questions

strengths: Novel contribution identifying important gap between VLM accuracy and reasoning explainability in geolocation task
High-quality dataset sourced from genuine domain experts (top 0.01% GeoGuessr players) with clear annotation guidelines
Rigorous experimental design with human validation (ICC 0.71-0.92), appropriate baselines, and cross-validation
Comprehensive evaluation spanning multiple model families (8-9 models, open-weight and proprietary)
Insightful five-category taxonomy of VLM failure modes with concrete illustrations, particularly valuable insights about lossy image encoding and missed fine-grained details
Three distinct automated evaluation approaches with algorithmic documentation and statistical reporting with confidence intervals
Clear commitment to open-source benchmark and evaluation code enabling reproducibility
Well-written presentation with effective use of examples and pedagogical figures (especially Figure 12)
weaknesses: Limited expert annotation scale: only 3 experts and human validation on 150/500 locations (30%); inter-annotator agreement only computed on validation subset, not full 800 chains

Moderate automated-to-human grading agreement (Pearson r=0.689) indicating ~31% disagreement not adequately discussed; choice of one-to-all over keypoint method based on MAE/Pearson could be better justified
Evaluation metric (F1 on reasoning chains) is novel but validation as measure of 'reasoning quality' is limited; no downstream task validation
Fundamental non-exhaustiveness problem: different valid reasoning paths could yield different F1 scores, creating inherent ambiguity; no analysis of alternative valid chains
Fixed prompt across all VLMs despite acknowledging it disadvantages some models; no prompt optimization or judge sensitivity analysis performed

Geographic distribution inherently biased by Street View coverage (Figure 4 shows clear concentration); no analysis of whether results generalize to underrepresented regions; only Street View images studied

Large expert-to-VLM accuracy gap (56.69 vs 43.74) but inconsistent with expert country-level performance (96-97%), suggesting experts use substantial tacit knowledge not captured in chains; gap not explored
Limited comparative analysis: no per-model error pattern analysis, per-attribute category difficulty analysis, or per-region failure breakdown; unclear which VLMs suitable for downstream applications
Scope limitations: English-only chains, geolocation-specific task; generalization to other reasoning domains or image modalities unexplored
Missing downstream validation: no evidence that F1 scores predict utility for non-experts or downstream tasks; benchmark assumes F1 = reasoning quality without empirical validation
